accepted.s: Which one of the following appellate tribunals was abolished under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021?
accepted.x: The Film Certification Appellate Tribunal was among the appellate tribunals abolished under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
accepted.tq: Identify the exact body abolished rather than confusing it with a continuing tribunal.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding bodies abolished under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021:
1. The Intellectual Property Appellate Board was abolished.
2. The Airport Appellate Tribunal was abolished.
3. The Authority for Advance Rulings (Customs) was abolished.
4. The Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal was abolished.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: All four bodies listed were abolished. Their appellate or adjudicatory functions were shifted as provided in the reforms framework, with several functions moving to High Courts.
accepted.tq: Use the complete list to distinguish abolished specialised tribunals from continuing bodies.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: After the abolition of the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Airport Appellate Tribunal, their functions were primarily shifted to the:
accepted.x: The functions of the dissolved appellate tribunals were moved to the High Courts.
accepted.tq: Test the institutional destination of transferred functions.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: Under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, which one of the following correctly describes the tenure and age framework?
o: Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; all members up to 70 years
Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; Chairperson up to 70 years and members up to 67 years
Tenure of five years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; Chairperson up to 67 years
Tenure of three years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; members up to 65 years
accepted.x: The 2021 framework prescribed a four-year tenure, a minimum appointment age of 50 years, a maximum age of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for members.
accepted.tq: Split the option into tenure, minimum age and maximum-age components.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s:
The Supreme Court’s Madras Bar Association ruling in 2025 struck down which of the following provisions associated with the tribunal framework?
1. Minimum appointment age of 50 years
2. Four-year tenure
3. The provision equating tribunal members with civil servants
4. The arrangement under which the Search-cum-Selection Committee sent two names
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The ruling struck down the minimum age of 50 years, the four-year tenure and the provision equating members with civil servants. It also replaced the two-name recommendation arrangement with one name per vacancy.
accepted.tq: Check each separate consequence of the judicial ruling instead of relying on a single headline fact.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: Which one of the following changes followed the Supreme Court’s 2025 ruling concerning the Search-cum-Selection Committee for tribunal appointments?
o: It was required to send one name per vacancy.
It was permitted to send two names for every vacancy.
It was required to send three names for every vacancy.
It was abolished and replaced by direct appointment by the Finance Ministry.
accepted.x: The earlier arrangement of sending two names was replaced by a requirement to send one name per vacancy.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the closely related figures two names and one name.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: The Supreme Court, in its 2025 Madras Bar Association ruling, directed the government to establish a National Tribunals Commission within:
accepted.x: The Supreme Court directed the government to establish a National Tribunals Commission within four months.
accepted.tq: Test the precise time limit rather than the broad subject of the judgment.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Introduction of the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 in the Lok Sabha
B. Passage of the Bill by the Lok Sabha by voice vote
C. Passage of the Bill by the Rajya Sabha
D. Supreme Court’s Madras Bar Association ruling
accepted.x: The 2025 Supreme Court ruling preceded the 2026 Bill; the Bill was passed by the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026 and by the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026. The notes identify its introduction before Lok Sabha passage.
accepted.tq: Fix the 2025 event first, then place the two House votes in date order.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: The Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026 through a:
o: Division vote after a constitutional amendment
accepted.x: The Lok Sabha passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 by voice vote on 10 August 2026.
accepted.tq: Test the exact parliamentary procedure attached to the date.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: Who moved the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 in Parliament?
o: The Chairperson of the Law Commission
accepted.x: The Bill was moved by Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal.
accepted.tq: Apply the who-did-what trap to distinguish the moving minister from other legal authorities.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched with the National Tribunals Commission proposed under the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026?
o: Technical members — Two persons with at least 25 years’ experience
Chairperson — Former Supreme Court judge or former Chief Justice of a High Court
Tenure — Four years irrespective of age
accepted.x: The proposed tenure is five years or until the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier, not four years irrespective of age.
accepted.tq: Find the single altered numerical provision in an otherwise correctly matched list.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s:
With reference to the National Tribunals Commission proposed in the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026, consider the following statements:
1. It is proposed to have its headquarters at New Delhi.
2. It is proposed to have two judicial and two technical members in addition to the Chairperson.
3. Its functions include tribunal appointments, performance review and disciplinary inquiries.
4. Its Chairperson must be a serving judge of the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. The Chairperson may be a former Supreme Court judge or a former High Court Chief Justice; the office is not restricted to a serving Supreme Court judge.
accepted.tq: Reject the over-specific authority qualification while retaining the organisational details.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: Which of the following correctly represents the proposed composition of the National Tribunals Commission under the 2026 Bill?
o: A Chairperson, three judicial members and one technical member
A Chairperson, two judicial members and two technical members
A Chairperson and four technical members only
Two Chairpersons, two judicial members and one technical member
accepted.x: The proposed Commission consists of five persons: a Chairperson, two judicial members and two technical members.
accepted.tq: Count the composition carefully and distinguish the Chairperson from the four other members.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: Under the 2026 Bill, the tenure of the National Tribunals Commission is proposed to be:
o: Three years with no age limit
Five years or age 75 years, whichever is later
Four years or age 67 years, whichever is earlier
Five years or age 70 years, whichever is earlier
accepted.x: The proposed tenure is five years or until the age of 70 years, whichever is earlier.
accepted.tq: Compare both the duration and the age condition before selecting the option.
accepted.sec: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

accepted.s: State Administrative Tribunals are established by the Central Government:
o: Only on the recommendation of the Supreme Court
Only through a resolution of the State Legislative Council
At the request of the concerned State Government
Automatically in every State under Article 323B
accepted.x: A State Administrative Tribunal is set up by the Central Government at the request of the concerned State Government.
accepted.tq: Test the correct initiating authority and avoid swapping the Central and State roles.
accepted.sec: State Administrative Tribunals - APAT establishment and abolition history

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding joint administrative tribunals is correct?
o: They are established exclusively by the Supreme Court.
They can be established only when all States in India agree.
They can be established for two or more States.
They can be established only for Union Territories.
accepted.x: Joint tribunals may be established for two or more States.
accepted.tq: Use the scope of the institution to distinguish a joint tribunal from a State-specific tribunal.
accepted.sec: State Administrative Tribunals - APAT establishment and abolition history

accepted.s: The 32nd Constitutional Amendment, 1973 provided constitutional authority for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh under:
accepted.x: The 32nd Amendment inserted the constitutional basis under Article 371D for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh to deal with public-service grievances.
accepted.tq: Avoid the Article-number swap by linking the amendment with its specific regional provision.
accepted.sec: State Administrative Tribunals - APAT establishment and abolition history

accepted.s: The Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal contemplated under Article 371D was intended to deal primarily with:
accepted.x: The Article 371D tribunal was intended to adjudicate grievances relating to public services in Andhra Pradesh.
accepted.tq: Identify the subject-matter jurisdiction rather than the constitutional source alone.
accepted.sec: State Administrative Tribunals - APAT establishment and abolition history

accepted.s: A tribunal is best described as a body which is:
o: Quasi-judicial, lying between an executive body and a court
A legislative committee exercising delegated law-making power
A constitutional court equal in status to the Supreme Court
Purely executive and without adjudicatory functions
accepted.x: A tribunal is quasi-judicial: it is neither purely executive nor a regular court, but occupies an intermediate position between the two.
accepted.tq: Test the precise definition and reject the extreme classifications.
accepted.sec: Administrative adjudication - quasi-judicial bodies, merits, criticisms  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Which of the following is NOT generally regarded as a merit of administrative tribunals?
1. Expertise and specialisation
2. Speedier adjudication
3. Lower cost
4. Compulsory application of the full Civil Procedure Code
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: Expertise, specialisation, speed and lower cost are recognised merits. Tribunals follow principles of natural justice instead of being bound by the full application of the Civil Procedure Code.
accepted.tq: Find the exception by separating tribunal advantages from the procedural feature that does not apply.
accepted.sec: Administrative adjudication - quasi-judicial bodies, merits, criticisms  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following procedural approaches is associated with tribunals rather than strict ordinary-court procedure?
o: Application of natural justice instead of the Civil Procedure Code
accepted.x: Tribunals are valued for applying principles of natural justice rather than being bound by the full procedural requirements of the Civil Procedure Code.
accepted.tq: Recognise the practical procedural distinction between tribunals and ordinary courts.
accepted.sec: Administrative adjudication - quasi-judicial bodies, merits, criticisms  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which criticism of the tribunal system relates most directly to institutional independence?
o: The same ministries whose decisions are reviewed may administer the tribunals.
Tribunals are constitutionally prohibited from reviewing administrative action.
Tribunals cannot provide any form of adjudication.
accepted.x: A major criticism is that parent ministries, which may be litigants before tribunals, also administer them, creating concerns about executive control and independence.
accepted.tq: Match the criticism with the institutional conflict it describes.
accepted.sec: Administrative adjudication - quasi-judicial bodies, merits, criticisms  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Executive control over tribunals has been particularly criticised in connection with the:
o: Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Finance Commission Act, 1951
States Reorganisation Act, 1956 and the 73rd Amendment
Finance Act, 2017 and the Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021
accepted.x: The criticism of executive control has been associated with the Finance Act, 2017 and the Tribunals Reforms Ordinance, 2021.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the paired legislative measures linked to the criticism.
accepted.sec: Administrative adjudication - quasi-judicial bodies, merits, criticisms  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which statement best captures the constitutional position of tribunals in relation to High Courts?
o: Tribunal decisions remain subject to judicial review by High Courts.
Tribunals completely exclude the judicial-review jurisdiction of High Courts.
High Courts may review only the financial accounts of tribunals.
Tribunals may overrule constitutional decisions of High Courts.
accepted.x: Although tribunals provide specialised adjudication, their decisions remain subject to the judicial-review jurisdiction of High Courts.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute-exclusion trap in statements about judicial review.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: Which one of the following proposals relates to improving access to the tribunal system through a common filing mechanism?
o: Mandatory filing only through the Supreme Court registry
accepted.x: A national report on the tribunal system proposed universal filing on a Zero FIR-style model to improve access.
accepted.tq: Identify the distinctive reform proposal rather than a general procedural reform.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: The National Sports Tribunal, notified under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, provides for appeals to the:
accepted.x: Appeals from the National Sports Tribunal lie to the Supreme Court.
accepted.tq: Test the appellate forum and avoid confusing it with the High Court review route generally applicable to tribunals.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: For disputes relating to electoral rolls in West Bengal after the Special Intensive Revision, the Election Commission set up how many Appellate Tribunals under retired High Court judges?
accepted.x: The Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals under retired High Court judges for the West Bengal roll disputes.
accepted.tq: Recall the exact number and the institutional composition together.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Tribunal or water dispute)
a. Central Administrative Tribunal
b. Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal
c. Krishna-II Water Disputes Tribunal
d. Vansadhara Water Disputes Tribunal

List-II (Year)
i. 1985
ii. 1969
iii. 2004
iv. 2010

Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The Central Administrative Tribunal was established in 1985; the Godavari, Krishna-II and Vansadhara water tribunals are associated with 1969, 2004 and 2010 respectively.
accepted.tq: Start with the sure CAT–1985 pair and then match the three Andhra Pradesh water tribunals by year.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal, established in 1985, is regarded as the first tribunal under:
accepted.x: The Central Administrative Tribunal, established in 1985, was the first tribunal under Article 323A.
accepted.tq: Link the first-in-sequence fact with its correct constitutional provision.
accepted.sec: Universal angles

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Tribunals are intended to provide faster adjudication.
2. Tribunals are intended to bring specialised expertise into dispute resolution.
3. Tribunals are completely outside the supervisory jurisdiction of constitutional courts.
4. Parent ministries may face a conflict of interest when they administer tribunals dealing with their own decisions.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Tribunals remain subject to judicial review by High Courts, so statement 3 is false.
accepted.tq: Combine merits, criticism and the judicial-review safeguard, rejecting the absolute claim.
accepted.sec: Universal angles
